Lecture 14

Free fermions: the XY and transverse-field Ising chains

What this lecture does

Here is a chain of spins that looks interacting and is not. A change of variables due to Jordan and Wigner turns its spins into fermions, and the Hamiltonian into a quadratic form in them; Fourier and Bogoliubov then diagonalise it completely. The lecture does this by hand, including the one step that short accounts often drop: the chain splits into two sectors with different boundary conditions, and the spectrum comes out wrong without them. The result is the baseline for everything that follows. A free chain has a conserved occupation for every mode and no genuine scattering; whatever the Bethe ansatz of Lecture 15 buys, it buys relative to this.

Notes (PDF)

Reading and tutorial. Material marked Reading is studied on your own; material marked Tutorial is worked in the tutorial. Everything else is the lectured core.

14.1 The models

On a ring of NNN sites, each carrying a spin 12\tfrac1221​ with Pauli matrices σx,σy,σz\sigma^{x},\sigma^{y},\sigma^{z}σx,σy,σz, the transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) is H=−J∑n=1Nσnxσn+1x−h∑n=1Nσnz,J,h≥0,σN+1=σ1. H=-J\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sigma^{x}_n\sigma^{x}_{n+1}-h\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sigma^{z}_n, \qquad J,h\ge0,\qquad \sigma_{N+1}=\sigma_1 . H=−Jn=1∑N​σnx​σn+1x​−hn=1∑N​σnz​,J,h≥0,σN+1​=σ1​.(14.1) The first term wants neighbouring spins aligned along xxx; the second, the transverse field, wants every spin up along zzz. The two do not commute, and that competition is the whole model. NNN is even throughout. (For odd NNN the momentum k=πk=\pik=π moves from one of the grids of §14.4 to the other; nothing changes in principle, but the bookkeeping does, and it is not treated.)

Two limits by inspection. At J=0J=0J=0 the ground state is ∣↑↑⋯↑⟩\ket{\uparrow\uparrow\cdots\uparrow}∣↑↑⋯↑⟩ with energy −hN-hN−hN, and flipping one spin costs 2h2h2h. At h=0h=0h=0 there are two ground states, all spins along +x+x+x or all along −x-x−x, energy −JN-JN−JN; the cheapest excitation of a ring is a pair of domain walls, each breaking one bond at cost 2J2J2J, so 4J4J4J in all. Between the limits something must happen, and §14.5 finds it at h=Jh=Jh=J.

The symmetry. Let Π=∏n=1Nσnz. \Pi=\prod_{n=1}^{N}\sigma^{z}_n . Π=n=1∏N​σnz​.(14.2) Each σnz\sigma^{z}_nσnz​ commutes with the field term and anticommutes with σnx\sigma^{x}_nσnx​, so Π\PiΠ commutes with every bond σnxσn+1x\sigma^{x}_n\sigma^{x}_{n+1}σnx​σn+1x​ (two anticommutations) and with HHH. It is the spin flip σx→−σx\sigma^{x}\to-\sigma^{x}σx→−σx, it squares to 111, and it splits the Hilbert space into an even sector Π=+1\Pi=+1Π=+1 and an odd sector Π=−1\Pi=-1Π=−1. It exchanges the two h=0h=0h=0 ground states, so the combinations with a definite parity are their sum (even) and difference (odd).

The XY chain. The TFIM is one member of a family, HXY=−J∑n=1N(1+η2 σnxσn+1x+1−η2 σnyσn+1y)−h∑n=1Nσnz, H_{XY}=-J\sum_{n=1}^{N}\Big(\frac{1+\eta}{2}\,\sigma^{x}_n\sigma^{x}_{n+1} +\frac{1-\eta}{2}\,\sigma^{y}_n\sigma^{y}_{n+1}\Big)-h\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sigma^{z}_n, HXY​=−Jn=1∑N​(21+η​σnx​σn+1x​+21−η​σny​σn+1y​)−hn=1∑N​σnz​,(14.3) with anisotropy η\etaη; η=1\eta=1η=1 is the TFIM. (The literature writes γ\gammaγ for η\etaη; this course keeps γ\gammaγ for Lecture 19’s coupling.) Its solution is the same three steps as the TFIM’s, and it is stated, not solved: the result is the TFIM’s with the quasiparticle energy ε(k)=2(h−Jcos⁡k)2+η2J2sin⁡2k\varepsilon(k)=2\sqrt{(h-J\cos k)^{2}+\eta^{2}J^{2}\sin^{2}k}ε(k)=2(h−Jcosk)2+η2J2sin2k​ (the reading at the end of this lecture).

14.2 Fermions

The algebra

Definition 14.1 (Fermionic modes). Operators c1,…,cNc_1,\dots,c_Nc1​,…,cN​ on a Hilbert space satisfy the canonical anticommutation relations (CAR) if {cm,cn†}=δmn,{cm,cn}=0, \{c_m,c_n^{\dagger}\}=\delta_{mn},\qquad \{c_m,c_n\}=0, {cm​,cn†​}=δmn​,{cm​,cn​}=0,(14.4) where {A,B}=AB+BA\{A,B\}=AB+BA{A,B}=AB+BA. The operator nj=cj†cjn_j=c_j^{\dagger}c_jnj​=cj†​cj​ is the occupation of mode jjj, and Nf=∑jnjN_f=\sum_jn_jNf​=∑j​nj​ the fermion number.

Everything about these operators follows from (14.4). Taking m=nm=nm=n in the second relation gives cj2=0c_j^{2}=0cj2​=0 and (cj†)2=0(c_j^{\dagger})^{2}=0(cj†​)2=0: no mode can be created twice — Pauli’s principle. Then nj2=cj†(1−cj†cj)cj=njn_j^{2}=c_j^{\dagger}(1-c_j^{\dagger}c_j)c_j=n_jnj2​=cj†​(1−cj†​cj​)cj​=nj​, so each njn_jnj​ has eigenvalues 000 and 111, and the njn_jnj​ commute with each other.

Fock space. Suppose a unit vector ∣0⟩\ket0∣0⟩, the vacuum, has cj∣0⟩=0c_j\ket0=0cj​∣0⟩=0 for all jjj. The 2N2^{N}2N vectors cj1†cj2†⋯cjM†∣0⟩,j1<j2<⋯<jM,c^{\dagger}_{j_1}c^{\dagger}_{j_2}\cdots c^{\dagger}_{j_M}\ket0,\qquad j_1<j_2<\dots<j_M,cj1​†​cj2​†​⋯cjM​†​∣0⟩,j1​<j2​<⋯<jM​, are eigenvectors of every njn_jnj​, with nj=1n_j=1nj​=1 exactly for the jjj listed; they are orthonormal, their span is mapped to itself by every cjc_jcj​ and cj†c_j^{\dagger}cj†​, and the action there is fixed by the CAR alone. The order of the jjj’s matters only through a sign: c1†c2†∣0⟩=−c2†c1†∣0⟩c_1^{\dagger}c_2^{\dagger}\ket0=-c_2^{\dagger}c_1^{\dagger}\ket0c1†​c2†​∣0⟩=−c2†​c1†​∣0⟩. That sign is what makes fermions fermions, and it is where spins differ.

Spins are not fermions

On one site, σ+=∣↑⟩ ⁣⟨↓∣\sigma^{+}=\ket\uparrow\!\bra\downarrowσ+=∣↑⟩⟨↓∣ and σ−=∣↓⟩ ⁣⟨↑∣\sigma^{-}=\ket\downarrow\!\bra\uparrowσ−=∣↓⟩⟨↑∣ satisfy {σ−,σ+}=1\{\sigma^{-},\sigma^{+}\}=1{σ−,σ+}=1 and (σ−)2=0(\sigma^{-})^{2}=0(σ−)2=0: one spin is one fermionic mode, with ∣↑⟩\ket\uparrow∣↑⟩ empty and ∣↓⟩\ket\downarrow∣↓⟩ occupied. But on two different sites, σ1−\sigma^{-}_1σ1−​ and σ2−\sigma^{-}_2σ2−​ act on different tensor factors, so they commute; their anticommutator is 2σ1−σ2−≠02\sigma^{-}_1\sigma^{-}_2\ne02σ1−​σ2−​=0. Spin flips on different sites are hard-core bosons: they exclude each other on a site and commute between sites. The fix has to supply a minus sign whenever two flips are exchanged, and it cannot be local.

The boundary bond is the one term that is not a quadratic form in the ccc’s: it carries the parity of the whole chain. But Π\PiΠ commutes with HHH, so on each sector it is a number, and there the boundary term is quadratic after all. Define cN+1:=−c1c_{N+1}:=-c_1cN+1​:=−c1​ in the even sector and cN+1:=+c1c_{N+1}:=+c_1cN+1​:=+c1​ in the odd sector. Each H±H_{\pm}H±​ is quadratic, commutes with Π\PiΠ (every term changes NfN_fNf​ by 000 or ±2\pm2±2), and acts on all of Fock space. So the spectrum of HHH is found in two steps: diagonalise H+H_{+}H+​ and H−H_{-}H−​ completely, then keep the even states of the first and the odd states of the second. The half thrown away is not part of the spin chain.

This is the step that is easy to lose. Dropping the boundary term, or imposing one boundary condition on both sectors, gives a quadratic model that is simple and wrong; §14.4 checks the difference on the board.

14.4 Fourier and Bogoliubov

Two grids of momenta

In each sector the fermions obey cn+N=∓cnc_{n+N}=\mp c_ncn+N​=∓cn​, so the plane waves that respect this are eikne^{\ii kn}eikn with eikN=∓1e^{\ii kN}=\mp1eikN=∓1: even sector (NS): k∈{π(2m+1)N},odd sector (R): k∈{2πmN},m=0,…,N−1, \text{even sector (NS):}\ k\in\Big\{\tfrac{\pi(2m+1)}{N}\Big\},\qquad \text{odd sector (R):}\ k\in\Big\{\tfrac{2\pi m}{N}\Big\},\qquad m=0,\dots,N-1, even sector (NS): k∈{Nπ(2m+1)​},odd sector (R): k∈{N2πm​},m=0,…,N−1,(14.11) with kkk taken mod 2π2\pi2π. 14.5 The quantum phase transition

Gaps

From (14.15), ε(k)2−4(J−h)2=8Jh(1−cos⁡k)≥0, \varepsilon(k)^{2}-4(J-h)^{2}=8Jh(1-\cos k)\ge0, ε(k)2−4(J−h)2=8Jh(1−cosk)≥0,(14.20) so the cheapest quasiparticle, at k=0k=0k=0, costs 2∣J−h∣2\abs{J-h}2∣J−h∣: the quasiparticle gap. The many-body gap — the distance from the ground state to the next level of the chain — is a different number, because each sector keeps only one parity of quasiparticle number. Theorem 14.7 (Gaps of the TFIM). As N→∞N\to\inftyN→∞ through even values:

For N=8N=8N=8 and h=0.4Jh=0.4Jh=0.4J the numbers are: doublet splitting 2.6⋅10−4J2.6\cdot10^{-4}J2.6⋅10−4J, against a quasiparticle gap of 1.2J1.2J1.2J, and the next level 2.60J2.60J2.60J above the ground state, on its way to 4(J−h)=2.4J4(J-h)=2.4J4(J−h)=2.4J (check-l14-algebra.py). Two phases

The doublet is spontaneous symmetry breaking seen through a finite window. In the ordered phase h<Jh<Jh<J the even and odd ground states are the finite-NNN versions of ∣→→⋯ ⟩±∣←←⋯ ⟩\ket{\to\to\cdots}\pm\ket{\leftarrow\leftarrow\cdots}∣→→⋯⟩±∣←←⋯⟩; their splitting is the amplitude to tunnel between the two ordered states, which needs a domain wall to sweep round the whole ring — hence exponentially small. As N→∞N\to\inftyN→∞ they become degenerate, and their combinations break the Π\PiΠ symmetry, with ⟨σx⟩≠0\langle\sigma^{x}\rangle\ne0⟨σx⟩=0 (the reading computes it). In the disordered phase h>Jh>Jh>J the ground state is unique and gapped, and a quasiparticle is a dressed flipped spin.

Between the phases the ground-state energy per site, e0(h)=lim⁡N→∞E0+N=−12π∫0πε(k) dk, e_0(h)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{E_0^{+}}N=-\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi}\varepsilon(k)\,\dd k, e0​(h)=N→∞lim​NE0+​​=−2π1​∫0π​ε(k)dk,(14.22) is continuous and has a continuous first derivative, but its second derivative diverges at h=Jh=Jh=J, like 1πJln⁡∣h−J∣\frac1{\pi J}\ln\abs{h-J}πJ1​ln∣h−J∣ (Figure 14.5) sketched: near k=0k=0k=0 and h=Jh=Jh=J, ε≈2(h−J)2+J2k2\varepsilon\approx2\sqrt{(h-J)^{2}+J^{2}k^{2}}ε≈2(h−J)2+J2k2​, whose second hhh-derivative integrates to a logarithm. A non-analyticity of the ground-state energy is what a quantum phase transition is, and the closing gap is its signature. At h=Jh=Jh=J itself, ε(k)=4J∣sin⁡(k/2)∣\varepsilon(k)=4J\abs{\sin(k/2)}ε(k)=4J∣sin(k/2)∣ and e0=−4J/πe_0=-4J/\pie0​=−4J/π.

14.6 Why this is not the end

The conserved charges

§13.5 allowed a model to be called integrable, without any of its three criteria, if its charges are constructed directly; the TFIM is such a model. Every occupation γk†γk\gamma_k^{\dagger}\gamma_kγk†​γk​ commutes with H±H_{\pm}H±​, but a single one is not local. Local combinations exist: weighting the term of kkk in (14.14) by cos⁡mk\cos mkcosmk gives an operator that still commutes with H±H_{\pm}H±​, block by block, and whose coefficients are still trigonometric polynomials in kkk — a sum of fermion bilinears of range at most m+2m+2m+2. The first beyond HHH is, in spins, Q+=∑n=1N[J(σnxσn+1zσn+2x−σnz)−h(σnxσn+1x+σnyσn+1y)],[H,Q+]=0, Q_{+}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\Big[J\big(\sigma^{x}_n\sigma^{z}_{n+1}\sigma^{x}_{n+2}-\sigma^{z}_n\big) -h\big(\sigma^{x}_n\sigma^{x}_{n+1}+\sigma^{y}_n\sigma^{y}_{n+1}\big)\Big], \qquad \comm{H}{Q_{+}}=0, Q+​=n=1∑N​[J(σnx​σn+1z​σn+2x​−σnz​)−h(σnx​σn+1x​+σny​σn+1y​)],[H,Q+​]=0,(14.23) a local charge of range 333 (Definition 13.2; the tutorial, and checked exactly for N=6,8,10N=6,8,10N=6,8,10). Continuing in mmm gives about NNN local charges, as for XXX in §13.3; Lecture 23 uses them to say which combinations of the nkn_knk​ a relaxed state remembers.

Free is linear

A quadratic Hamiltonian makes the Heisenberg equations linear: dγk/dt=i[H,γk]=−iε(k)γk\dd\gamma_k/\dd t=\ii\comm{H}{\gamma_k}=-\ii\varepsilon(k)\gamma_kdγk​/dt=i[H,γk​]=−iε(k)γk​, so each mode turns at its own frequency and ignores the others — the quantum form of the linear flow φ˙=ν\dot\varphi=\freqφ˙​=ν on a torus, and the reason there is no scattering. In the XX chain (η=0\eta=0η=0), which conserves the fermion number, the MMM-fermion eigenstates are Slater determinants of plane waves. As fermions they do not scatter (S=1S=1S=1); as spin flips, hard-core bosons, two of them pick up only the exchange sign, S=−1S=-1S=−1, whatever their momenta. The periodicity condition of Lecture 15 sets eikjNe^{\ii k_jN}eikj​N equal to a product of two-body S-matrices, one for each other particle; with S=−1S=-1S=−1 it reads eikjN=(−1)M−1e^{\ii k_jN}=(-1)^{M-1}eikj​N=(−1)M−1: exactly the NS or R grid of the sector with parity (−1)M(-1)^{M}(−1)M (checked, N=8N=8N=8, M≤4M\le4M≤4). Boundary condition and exchange phase are one bookkeeping, and Lecture 15 meets it again with an SSS that depends on the momenta.

That dependence is what the TFIM lacks, and why the lecture is a baseline and not a template. Jordan–Wigner applied to the Heisenberg chain turns σnzσn+1z=(1−2nn)(1−2nn+1)\sigma^{z}_n\sigma^{z}_{n+1}=(1-2n_n)(1-2n_{n+1})σnz​σn+1z​=(1−2nn​)(1−2nn+1​) into a quartic term: the fermions interact, nothing linearises, and the next lecture needs a different method.

the linear action–angle system, K(I)=∑iνiIiK(I)=\sum_i\freq_iI_iK(I)=∑i​νi​Ii​: independent oscillators, each angle turning at a fixed frequency, and nothing scatters (§5.2) ⟶\longrightarrow⟶ free fermions, H=∑kε(k)(nk−12)H=\sum_k\varepsilon(k)(n_k-\tfrac 12)H=∑k​ε(k)(nk​−21​): independent modes, γk(t)=e−iε(k)tγk\gamma_k(t)=e^{-\ii\varepsilon(k)t}\gamma_kγk​(t)=e−iε(k)tγk​, two-body S-matrix ±1\pm 1±1 whatever the momenta (type A, structural analogy: the same role, no ℏ→0\hbar\to 0ℏ→0 limit taken)

The construction of local charges. Every occupation γk†γk\gamma_k^{\dagger}\gamma_kγk†​γk​ commutes with H±H_{\pm}H±​; the local charges come from weighting whole blocks: for an even function fff, weight the term of kkk in (14.14) by f(k)f(k)f(k). The odd combinations ∑ksin⁡mk ck†ck\sum_k\sin mk\,c_k^{\dagger}c_k∑k​sinmkck†​ck​ also commute, because pairing creates kkk and −k-k−k together and leaves nk−n−kn_k-n_{-k}nk​−n−k​ alone. In spin language the first few are these.

Proposition 14.9 (Local charges of the TFIM sketched). Beside HHH, the local charges (Definition 13.2) Q+=∑n=1N[J(σnxσn+1zσn+2x−σnz)−h(σnxσn+1x+σnyσn+1y)],Q−=∑n=1N(σnxσn+1y−σnyσn+1x),Q−′=∑n=1N(σnxσn+1zσn+2y−σnyσn+1zσn+2x)\begin{align*} Q_{+}&=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\Big[J\big(\sigma^{x}_n\sigma^{z}_{n+1}\sigma^{x}_{n+2}-\sigma^{z}_n\big) -h\big(\sigma^{x}_n\sigma^{x}_{n+1}+\sigma^{y}_n\sigma^{y}_{n+1}\big)\Big],\\ Q_{-}&=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\big(\sigma^{x}_n\sigma^{y}_{n+1}-\sigma^{y}_n\sigma^{x}_{n+1}\big),\qquad Q_{-}'=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\big(\sigma^{x}_n\sigma^{z}_{n+1}\sigma^{y}_{n+2}-\sigma^{y}_n\sigma^{z}_{n+1}\sigma^{x}_{n+2}\big) \end{align*}Q+​Q−​​=n=1∑N​[J(σnx​σn+1z​σn+2x​−σnz​)−h(σnx​σn+1x​+σny​σn+1y​)],=n=1∑N​(σnx​σn+1y​−σny​σn+1x​),Q−′​=n=1∑N​(σnx​σn+1z​σn+2y​−σny​σn+1z​σn+2x​)​ commute with HHH and with each other. Q+Q_{+}Q+​ is, in each sector, −2-2−2 times the f=cos⁡kf=\cos kf=cosk charge above, plus a constant. (The fermionic argument is the sketch; the commutators are checked exactly for N=6,8,10N=6,8,10N=6,8,10.)

At N=8N=8N=8 and h=0.7Jh=0.7Jh=0.7J a computer search (the check script) finds that, modulo multiples of the identity, the conserved local charges of range at most three are spanned by HHH, Q+Q_{+}Q+​, Q−Q_{-}Q−​, Q−′Q_{-}'Q−′​ — at that size and coupling only. Spin forms follow from (14.8) and its analogues: a fermion bilinear on sites nnn and n+dn+dn+d carries the string of the d−1d-1d−1 sites between them, and on the ring the terms that wrap round pick up −Π-\Pi−Π exactly as the boundary bond did, so one spin operator serves both sectors.

Reading

14.8 The XY chain, and duality as a map

The XY chain (14.3) goes through the same three steps, with the same sectors and grids, and gives Theorem 14.6 with ε(k)=2(h−Jcos⁡k)2+η2J2sin⁡2k, \varepsilon(k)=2\sqrt{(h-J\cos k)^{2}+\eta^{2}J^{2}\sin^{2}k}, ε(k)=2(h−Jcosk)2+η2J2sin2k​,(14.24) and signed e0e_0e0​, eπe_\pieπ​ unchanged (checked against exact diagonalisation at N=8N=8N=8 by the check script; the derivation is Sheet 14). The gap closes where both squares vanish: on the line h=Jh=Jh=J, and on the segment η=0\eta=0η=0, h≤Jh\le Jh≤J, where ε\varepsilonε vanishes at cos⁡k=h/J\cos k=h/Jcosk=h/J (Figure 14.6). At η=0\eta=0η=0 the chain is the XX chain, which conserves the number of fermions; it reappears in §14.6.

Duality. Behind this is an exact map of operators (Kramers and Wannier 1941, for the classical two-dimensional Ising model) cited: the domain-wall variables τz=σnxσn+1x\tau^{z}=\sigma^{x}_n\sigma^{x}_{n+1}τz=σnx​σn+1x​ living on the bonds turn the bond term into a field and the field into a bond term, exchanging the ordered and disordered phases. It does not map the odd sector to itself — the signed mode e0=2(h−J)e_0=2(h-J)e0​=2(h−J) changes sign — which is why the proposition says “even”. Kramers and Wannier’s use of it survives intact: if there is one transition, it must be at the self-dual point.

Reading

14.9 Correlations as a Toeplitz determinant

Write An=cn†+cnA_n=c_n^{\dagger}+c_nAn​=cn†​+cn​ and Bn=cn†−cnB_n=c_n^{\dagger}-c_nBn​=cn†​−cn​, so that An2=1A_n^{2}=1An2​=1, Bn2=−1B_n^{2}=-1Bn2​=−1, and a bulk bond is σnxσn+1x=BnAn+1\sigma^{x}_n\sigma^{x}_{n+1}=B_nA_{n+1}σnx​σn+1x​=Bn​An+1​ by (14.8). Since (σx)2=1(\sigma^{x})^{2}=1(σx)2=1, σ1xσ1+rx=(σ1xσ2x)(σ2xσ3x)⋯(σrxσr+1x)=B1A2B2A3⋯BrAr+1,\sigma^{x}_1\sigma^{x}_{1+r}=(\sigma^{x}_1\sigma^{x}_2)(\sigma^{x}_2\sigma^{x}_3)\cdots (\sigma^{x}_r\sigma^{x}_{r+1})=B_1A_2B_2A_3\cdots B_rA_{r+1},σ1x​σ1+rx​=(σ1x​σ2x​)(σ2x​σ3x​)⋯(σrx​σr+1x​)=B1​A2​B2​A3​⋯Br​Ar+1​, a product of 2r2r2r fermion operators. In a Bogoliubov vacuum (a Gaussian state) such an expectation value is given by Wick’s theorem as a Pfaffian of two-point functions, and because ⟨AlAm⟩=δlm\langle A_lA_m\rangle=\delta_{lm}⟨Al​Am​⟩=δlm​ and ⟨BlBm⟩=−δlm\langle B_lB_m\rangle=-\delta_{lm}⟨Bl​Bm​⟩=−δlm​ it collapses to a determinant (Lieb, Schultz and Mattis 1961) cited: ⟨σ1xσ1+rx⟩=det⁡[g(m−l+1)]l,m=1r,g(d)=⟨BnAn+d⟩=12π∫−ππe−ikd Jeik−h∣Jeik−h∣ dk\langle\sigma^{x}_1\sigma^{x}_{1+r}\rangle=\det\big[g(m-l+1)\big]_{l,m=1}^{r},\qquad g(d)=\langle B_nA_{n+d}\rangle=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{-\ii kd}\, \frac{Je^{\ii k}-h}{\abs{Je^{\ii k}-h}}\,\dd k⟨σ1x​σ1+rx​⟩=det[g(m−l+1)]l,m=1r​,g(d)=⟨Bn​An+d​⟩=2π1​∫−ππ​e−ikd∣Jeik−h∣Jeik−h​dk in the thermodynamic limit (for finite NNN the integral is the average over the NS grid). A matrix whose entries depend only on m−lm-lm−l is a Toeplitz matrix, and the large-rrr behaviour of Toeplitz determinants is a classical subject (Szegő’s theorem and its extensions). The results, due to Pfeuty (1970) and, for the XY chain, Barouch and McCoy (1971) cited: for h<Jh<Jh<J the correlation tends to (1−h2/J2)1/4(1-h^{2}/J^{2})^{1/4}(1−h2/J2)1/4, so the spontaneous magnetisation is ⟨σx⟩=(1−h2/J2)1/8\langle\sigma^{x}\rangle=(1-h^{2}/J^{2})^{1/8}⟨σx⟩=(1−h2/J2)1/8; at h=Jh=Jh=J it decays like r−1/4r^{-1/4}r−1/4; for h>Jh>Jh>J it decays exponentially. The check script confirms the determinant formula against exact diagonalisation at N=12N=12N=12, and the ordered-phase limit at r=200r=200r=200 to six digits. Franchini’s Chapter 1 and its appendices carry this out in full.

Reading

14.10 The open chain and Majorana edge modes

Cut the ring: drop the boundary bond. There is then no parity-dependent term, no sectors, and one quadratic Hamiltonian on all of Fock space. Rewrite each fermion as two Hermitian Majorana operators, αn=cn+cn†\alpha_n=c_n+c_n^{\dagger}αn​=cn​+cn†​ and βn=i(cn−cn†)\beta_n=\ii(c_n-c_n^{\dagger})βn​=i(cn​−cn†​), with αn2=βn2=1\alpha_n^{2}=\beta_n^{2}=1αn2​=βn2​=1 and all different ones anticommuting. By (14.8) and 1−2nn=iαnβn1-2n_n=\ii\alpha_n\beta_n1−2nn​=iαn​βn​, Hopen=−iJ∑n=1N−1βnαn+1−ih∑n=1Nαnβn.H_{\mathrm{open}}=-\ii J\sum_{n=1}^{N-1}\beta_n\alpha_{n+1}-\ii h\sum_{n=1}^{N}\alpha_n\beta_n .Hopen​=−iJn=1∑N−1​βn​αn+1​−ihn=1∑N​αn​βn​. Each fermion is split in two, the field pairs the two halves on one site and the bond pairs halves on neighbouring sites. At h=0h=0h=0 the bonds pair βn\beta_nβn​ with αn+1\alpha_{n+1}αn+1​, and two Majoranas are left over, α1\alpha_1α1​ at the left end and βN\beta_NβN​ at the right, appearing nowhere in HHH. The fermion f=12(α1+iβN)f=\tfrac12(\alpha_1+\ii\beta_N)f=21​(α1​+iβN​) commutes with HHH: it costs zero energy, every level is exactly doubly degenerate, and the two halves of this zero mode sit at opposite ends of the chain. In spin language these are, again, the two ferromagnets. For 0<h<J0<h<J0<h<J the zero mode survives with an energy exponentially small in NNN (the check script measures (h/J)N(h/J)^{N}(h/J)N), localised near the ends; for h>Jh>Jh>J it is gone. This is Kitaev’s chain (2001) cited, a model of a one-dimensional ppp-wave superconductor: in the fermion language the ground-state doublet stays split only exponentially under sufficiently weak local perturbations that conserve fermion parity and do not close the bulk gap (a physical perturbation of fermions always conserves parity; the exact pairing of every level at h=0h=0h=0 is not what is protected), while in the spin language a weak longitudinal field σx\sigma^{x}σx, which is local for spins, splits it at once. The same algebra, read in two languages, gives a fragile symmetry breaking and a robust topological degeneracy (Franchini, §1.5).

Summary

  • Jordan–Wigner: cn=(∏m<nσmz)σn+c_n=\big(\prod_{m<n}\sigma^{z}_m\big)\sigma^{+}_ncn​=(∏m<n​σmz​)σn+​ satisfies the CAR (Theorem 14.3); a fermion is a down spin, and Π=∏σz=(−1)Nf\Pi=\prod\sigma^{z}=(-1)^{N_f}Π=∏σz=(−1)Nf​.
  • The boundary term: σNxσ1x=−Π(cN†−cN)(c1†+c1)\sigma^{x}_N\sigma^{x}_1=-\Pi(c_N^{\dagger}-c_N)(c_1^{\dagger}+c_1)σNx​σ1x​=−Π(cN†​−cN​)(c1†​+c1​) (Proposition 14.4), so the fermions are antiperiodic in the even sector (NS momenta) and periodic in the odd one (R momenta).
  • The spectrum: ε(k)=2J2+h2−2Jhcos⁡k\varepsilon(k)=2\sqrt{J^{2}+h^{2}-2Jh\cos k}ε(k)=2J2+h2−2Jhcosk​; each sector’s levels are ∑εk(nk−12)\sum\varepsilon_k(n_k-\tfrac12)∑εk​(nk​−21​) with the sector’s parity, the R sector’s unpaired modes carrying the signed 2(h∓J)2(h\mp J)2(h∓J) (Theorem 14.6).
  • The transition at h=Jh=Jh=J: quasiparticle gap 2∣J−h∣2\abs{J-h}2∣J−h∣; for h>Jh>Jh>J a many-body gap 2(h−J)2(h-J)2(h−J); for h<Jh<Jh<J a doublet, exponentially split, and a gap 4(J−h)4(J-h)4(J−h) above it (Theorem 14.7); e0′′e_0''e0′′​ diverges logarithmically; self-dual under J↔hJ\leftrightarrow hJ↔h (Proposition 14.8).
  • Free means linear: local charges are fermion bilinears ((14.23)), modes evolve independently, and the two-body S-matrix is ±1\pm1±1, independent of momenta. The Bethe ansatz starts where this stops.
